articles.headline: Schools Ask FCC Not to End Program That Pays For the Internet They Are Asked to Use Less
articles.dek: Libraries, principals and even the cable lobby tell the FCC that E-Rate, a roughly $2 billion-a-year connectivity program, is not finished just because the wires now exist.
articles.catch_up: E-Rate, created by Congress in the 1996 telecommunications law, discounts internet service and network equipment for schools and libraries. In June, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr led a 2-1 vote to seek comment on whether the program should be limited or sunset.
articles.why_it_matters: If E-Rate shrinks or disappears, schools and libraries would have to cover internet costs from local budgets, or cut programs. Because the program is funded by fees on phone companies that usually appear on consumer bills, the debate also touches what households pay.
body: Schools and libraries across the country told the Federal Communications Commission this week that they would prefer to keep E-Rate, according to Ars Technica. The program distributes more than $2 billion a year to help pay for broadband and network equipment. The FCC asked whether it should be limited or ended, and the public has now answered at some length.

Carr has argued that E-Rate drifted beyond its original purpose of basic internet access for educational use, and criticized districts for having "experimented with a massive increase in screen time for students." The proposal asks whether the program should be "limited or sunset to reflect today's extensive connectivity rates." Translation: the internet now reaches most schools, so perhaps the program that put it there can retire. The commenters replied that the bills for it still arrive monthly.

That is the core of the filings. Rock Valley Christian School in Iowa, per principal Paul Lapka, estimates its annual internet cost at about $3,120 and its E-Rate support at about $1,560. Half the bill, in other words, is the difference between reliable service and what Lapka called "higher local costs, delayed network upgrades" and pressure to redirect money from other priorities. The Texas Library Association added that only 35 percent of the state's public libraries receive E-Rate discounts, against 65 percent nationally, which it called evidence of unmet need rather than a need that has passed.

There is also a legal question. The American Library Association told the FCC that it lacks authority to terminate a program mandated by Congress, and that it is responsible only for administering it. Ars Technica noted that Carr could respond by arguing the original mission is complete, which would make ending the program a matter of paperwork rather than defiance. The FCC's own proposal asks whether the program has fulfilled that mission. Translation: the agency is asking whether a job can be declared done by the agency that would then be relieved of doing it.

The ALA also argued that the FCC lacks the authority and expertise to regulate screen time, and that US law leaves decisions about inappropriate content to school boards and libraries. Commissioner Anna Gomez, who voted against the proposal, put it more briefly: the FCC is not the nation's parent, teacher or school board. The Carr FCC has already cut E-Rate support for lending Wi-Fi hotspots and for Wi-Fi on school buses.

An unusual ally appeared in the docket: the cable industry. America's Communications Association argued that schools must keep paying for broadband and replacing equipment. Ending E-Rate would mean fewer purchases from the companies that sell the service, which Ars Technica said would upset broadband providers. It is rare for a lobbying group and a library association to agree that customers should continue receiving discounts.

Reply comments follow the first round, after which the FCC decides whether to proceed. The program has a funding cap of $5.2 billion, though actual payouts depend on demand and approvals. For now, the only consensus is that the internet is everywhere, and that someone still has to pay for it.
articles.wire_headline: Schools across US protest FCC plan that could disconnect kids from Internet

articles.headline: Anthropic Warns Your Smart Fridge May Soon Be Recruited Into Malware
articles.dek: The AI company says small models could self-replicate across cheap IoT devices by next year, though its own experiment found plenty of obstacles.
articles.catch_up: Anthropic published research on whether small, open-weight AI models could run across low-cost internet-connected devices and spread without human help. Ars Technica reported that the experiment showed real promise for attackers but also significant challenges.
articles.why_it_matters: Millions of cheap, rarely updated gadgets sit on home networks, and a worm that can work out unfamiliar hardware on its own would be harder to defend against and harder to shut down. The findings are a warning about what may come, not a description of an attack under way.
body: Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could, as soon as next year, let malware copy itself across smart fridges, vacuum cleaners and other Internet of Things devices, Ars Technica reported. The company's own experiment turned up significant obstacles, so the warning is hedged. Still, it is the first time the kitchen appliance has been described as a potential recruit.

Some background. A computer worm is malware that spreads on its own, without anyone clicking a suspicious link. Translation: it does not need you to make a mistake, which is a relief to people who have been blamed for all of them. The new concern is a worm that carries an AI model with it and uses the model to work out what device it has landed on.

Anthropic's researchers ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other IoT hardware. Open-weight means the model's trained parameters are publicly downloadable, so anyone can run the thing without asking permission. The trick was quantization, which means storing the model with fewer bits, and splitting the work into shards spread across devices. Translation: if one gadget is too small to hold a brain, several can share one.

The numbers are modest, which is rather the point. According to Ars Technica, the Gemma4-26B-A4B model achieved inference, meaning its weights loaded and it could generate output, using just 15 boxes with only 4GB of memory each. Separately, the Qwen3.5-9B model was able to configure other LLMs to run on eight of nine hardware types. Fifteen cheap boxes is not a data center. It is roughly what a determined person might find in a drawer of unwanted electronics.

What separates this from ordinary malware is adaptability. Traditional malware must be written for specific hardware or software, so attackers have to know their targets in advance. In Anthropic's test, the model used its weights to make configurations on the fly for the devices it faced. In other words, the malware reads the manual so the author does not have to.

Takedown is the second worry. Anthropic wrote that such a replicator would be challenging to shut down because there is no centralized point to switch off, though it might be slow, with a doubling time of days. Slow is comforting only in the way a slow leak is comforting. Without a central server, defenders cannot seize one domain and call it a day.

Anthropic is also candid that its experiment revealed significant challenges in actually building such a replicator, and the company presents the finding as tempered. That caveat deserves weight: nothing described is a working outbreak. The more useful reading is as an early notice to device makers, who have a long record of shipping gadgets with weak security and little interest in updating them.

The thing to watch is whether manufacturers of low-cost devices treat a year's notice as a deadline or as a suggestion. Based on the industry's history with firmware updates, the vacuum cleaner is not holding its breath.
articles.wire_headline: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices

articles.headline: Windows Gets Two-Click AI Agents, Faster Start Menu, and a Slider for Memory
articles.dek: Microsoft and Nvidia launched RTX Spark laptops built on Arm chips, while Microsoft separately says Windows 11 is up to 20 percent more responsive after months of fixes.
articles.catch_up: Nvidia's RTX Spark laptops pair an Arm CPU with a Blackwell GPU and unified memory, and Microsoft has spent months tuning Windows for them. Separately, Microsoft promised earlier this year to fix Windows 11's performance and reliability.
articles.why_it_matters: If you buy a Windows laptop, the software may now run better on modest hardware, and a new class of Arm machines wants to run AI models and games locally. Some headline features, including Recall, are still missing at launch.
body: Microsoft and Nvidia held a launch event in San Francisco for the first RTX Spark laptops, which look like ordinary Windows machines but run on Arm chips rather than the x64 designs from Intel and AMD, according to The Verge. Translation: x64 and Arm are two different languages for telling a processor what to do, and most Windows software was written in the first one. Microsoft's solution is to translate in real time and hope nobody notices.

That translation is done by an emulator called Prism, which handles apps that lack a native Arm version. Peter Dawoud, a Microsoft principal program manager, told The Verge that "Emulation isn't generic. Each platform needs tuning." Microsoft says it ships a compatibility update every month, which is a polite way of saying the translator is still learning idioms.

The pitch is local AI. Windows on RTX Spark has a Get Started experience that lets users find and install an AI agent in two clicks. Translation: an agent is an AI program that does tasks for you, and local means it runs on your laptop rather than in someone else's data center. Hermes, Perplexity and OpenClaw are the first three officially supported. The reviewer found Hermes mostly two clicks, while OpenClaw complained about a local gateway until he uninstalled and reinstalled it, so the count is closer to two clicks plus one existential reinstall.

The reviewer also noted that large local models respond more slowly than cloud ones, so he expects to use them for overnight or background work. A laptop that thinks while you sleep is a fine product, though it is not quite the instant assistant the marketing implies.

Memory is the other selling point. Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra can ship with up to 128GB of unified memory, meaning the CPU and GPU share one pool, which lets huge models fit. Microsoft says it holds back a little so the system stays responsive. Machines with 24GB or 32GB get a slider in Nvidia's Windows app to shift memory toward the GPU, a tool for deciding which of your programs deserves to be starved.

Gaming is where Arm laptops have historically stalled, partly because anti-cheat software refused to cooperate. Fortnite, Marvel Rivals, Arc Raiders, Counter-Strike 2 and Dota 2 are supported out of the box. Call of Duty's anti-cheat arrives at some point in 2027, Battlefield's in early 2027, and PUBG in the first half of 2027. Riot has committed to League of Legends and Valorant with no date. The reviewer reached a stable 60fps in most games at medium settings, 1440p and DLSS performance, which is below a dedicated gaming laptop. Microsoft and Nvidia say these are not gaming machines, then list the games.

Not everything shipped. Copilot Plus PC features such as Recall are absent at launch, and Microsoft's Adrienne Brewbaker said they are expected to reach Windows Insiders later this year. It is not clear why they are delayed. Recall's absence may disappoint some buyers and relieve others.

Meanwhile, Microsoft says months of fixes have made Windows 11 up to 20 percent more responsive. Navjot Virk, a Microsoft corporate vice president, said Windows can now keep up to 2GB more active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage. On PCs with 8GB or less, Widgets load only when opened, freeing more than 200MB. Microsoft also let the taskbar move to the sides or top of the screen, a feature the world has requested since roughly the first taskbar.

Other fixes include a less disruptive Windows Update, faster Windows Hello sign-in, and an AirPods pairing experience up to 15 seconds faster. A faster Search is available to Insiders and is due to roll out more broadly later this year. The overall message is that Windows is getting leaner on cheap machines and ambitious on expensive ones, and the 8GB owner now gets some of the benefit.
articles.wire_headline: How Windows is being optimized for Nvidia’s RTX Spark laptops

articles.headline: Inflation Hits 3.7% as Gasoline Does Most of the Work and Everyone Feigns Surprise
articles.dek: September consumer prices rose 0.6% on a 9.1% jump in gasoline, strengthening bets that the Fed will raise rates again after its first hike in over three years.
articles.catch_up: Consumer prices have risen faster than the Fed's 2% goal since March 2021, and a U.S.-Iran war launched in late February sent energy costs sharply higher. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in more than three years.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher inflation means paychecks buy less, and the likely Fed response, more rate hikes, makes borrowing costlier. With midterms next month, the price of a gallon of gas is also a political variable.
body: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday that the consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.6% in September, putting the annual rate at 3.7%, up from 3.4% in August, according to CNBC. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had expected 0.6% and 3.6%, so the economy missed the forecast by one-tenth of a percentage point, which in this business counts as a plot twist.

The main culprit was energy. Gasoline rose 9.1% in a single month and accounted for about half of the headline gain, per the BLS. Over the past year gas is up 34.2% and fuel oil 74.2%. Translation: the thing you put in the car and the thing some people put in the furnace now cost roughly a third and nearly three-quarters more, respectively.

Strip out food and energy and you get core CPI, a measure designed to show underlying inflation by ignoring the items people actually buy most often. It rose 0.3% for the month and 2.6% annually, slightly above forecasts. Food was flat, shelter rose 0.4%, used vehicles rose 0.7%, and apparel, which is sensitive to tariffs, rose 0.3% and is up 3.4% on the year.

Markets reacted as markets do. Stock futures turned negative and bond yields rose sharply, per CNBC. Traders put the odds of a rate hike at the Fed's Oct. 27-28 meeting at about 54%, and the odds of one by year-end above 96%. Fed officials have lately suggested no need to rush, but most expect another increase this year.

The Fed's dilemma is a classic one. Energy shocks are usually treated as temporary, and central banks tend to look through them, which is a polite way of saying they squint and wait. But the longer the war lasts, the more likely higher prices seep into everything else and into what people expect to happen next. CNBC reported that Brent crude rose more than 14% in September and traded around $105 a barrel the day before the release.

Expectations are the real worry. CNBC noted that CPI has now run above 2% for about 65 consecutive months, the longest such streak of this century. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack warned that consumers are starting to accept high inflation as a fact of life, which she called concerning. If workers demand bigger raises and businesses raise prices ahead of costs, inflation can feed itself, and the Fed's tools work less well.

For households, the arithmetic is unkind. Inflation has recently outrun wage growth, so the average consumer has lost purchasing power, according to CNBC. The University of Michigan's survey reported record shares of people blaming high prices for worse finances. Economists quoted do not expect prices to fall back, since falling prices would signal something worse. The realistic hope is for wages to outpace inflation long enough to catch up.

The political calendar adds flavor. This was the last CPI report before the November midterms, and sentiment has fallen more among Republicans and independents than Democrats this year, per Michigan data. The Fed insists it does not consider elections. Voters, for their part, are considering very little else besides groceries and gas.

Next up is Thursday's producer price index, which forecasters expect to show wholesale prices up 5.5% from a year earlier. That is the figure retailers will eventually describe to you as someone else's decision.
articles.wire_headline: Consumer prices rose 3.7% annually in September as gas prices skyrocket

articles.headline: Wholesale Prices Jump 6.3%, Fed Funds Traders Discover Rate Hikes Exist
articles.dek: September's producer price index rose 1.3% on the month, more than double forecasts, as the Iran war's energy shock spread into diesel, goods and the Fed's calendar.
articles.catch_up: The U.S. is in a war with Iran that has curtailed Middle East oil supply and pushed energy prices sharply higher. This week brought a run of inflation reports, including consumer prices on Wednesday and producer prices on Thursday.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher wholesale costs tend to reach store shelves, and a hotter inflation picture raises the odds the Fed lifts borrowing costs, which affects mortgages, credit cards and business loans. The data also lands just before the midterm elections.
body: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday that its producer price index rose 1.3% in September and 6.3% from a year earlier, according to CNBC. Economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast 0.6% and 5.5%. In forecasting terms, this is what is known as a miss, and in household terms it is what is known as the bill.

Translation: the producer price index measures what businesses receive for goods and services at the wholesale level, before a retailer adds its own markup and a sad little sign about supply chains. When wholesale prices rise, the cost tends to be passed along, with the speed of a rumor and the generosity of a toll booth.

Energy did much of the work, as the conflict with Iran curtailed oil supply. Brent crude stood at 125.44 as of Oct. 6, per the latest official data. The more interesting detail is the spread: the BLS said almost half of September's rise in processed goods for immediate demand was tied to diesel prices. Diesel moves trucks, trucks move everything, and so a war far away ends up in the price of nearly anything that sits on a pallet.

Core PPI, which strips out food and energy because they are considered volatile, still rose 0.7% on the month and 5% over 12 months. Translation: removing the part of inflation officials like to call temporary leaves a part that is not behaving like a guest who plans to leave.

Wednesday's consumer price index showed prices up 0.6% on the month and 3.7% on the year, slightly above the 3.6% forecast. Core CPI rose 0.3% against an expected 0.2%. Wednesday's Beige Book, the Fed's anecdotal tour of the economy, contained the most inflation-related terms on record, according to Bespoke Investment Group. The central bank's own reading material is now essentially a complaint thread.

Consumers are holding up, but with visible effort. Retail sales rose 0.8% in September, beating the 0.4% forecast, yet excluding autos and gas stations the gain was about 0.25%, down from roughly 1.1% a month earlier. CNBC read this as a sign that shoppers are cutting back elsewhere to pay for fuel. Headline spending looks healthy partly because gasoline costs more, which is a bit like praising a restaurant for its rising bill.

The Fed's response is the part markets are now pricing in. CME's FedWatch tool put the chance of a rate hike on Oct. 28 at nearly 34%, up from under 18% a week earlier, and about 90% of traders expect at least one hike by year-end. Fed funds stand at 3.88%, while the 10-year Treasury yield is 5.21%, so bond investors have already moved ahead of the committee. Chris Zaccarelli of Northlight Asset Management said the Fed will have 'no choice' but to raise rates again this year.

Stocks, for their part, appear unbothered. The S&P 500 closed at 7718.94 as of Oct. 14, and the VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, sat at 16.87. Investors may know something, or may simply be waiting for the next data release to explain it. The next one arrives just before the midterms, which will determine who holds power in Washington, and who gets to explain prices to voters.
articles.wire_headline: Wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, biggest gain since 2022

articles.headline: AI Stocks Lose $1 Trillion in Four Days, Blame Interest Rates, China, and 2029
articles.dek: Twenty of the world's most valuable AI and chip stocks shed more than $1 trillion this week as borrowing costs rose and memory makers took the worst of it.
articles.catch_up: Chip and AI stocks had rallied for months on surging demand for data center hardware, with memory makers enjoying unprecedented price increases. This week, hot U.S. inflation data, rising Treasury yields and a Chinese memory announcement turned the mood sour.
articles.why_it_matters: The AI buildout is financed largely with borrowed money, so higher yields make it more expensive, and the stocks feeding it are a big part of many retirement portfolios. Whether the sell-off is a buying opportunity or a warning depends on whether demand actually weakens, and so far the evidence cited is mostly about financing.
body: Twenty of the most valuable AI and semiconductor stocks around the world have lost more than $1 trillion in combined value so far this week, CNBC reported. On Thursday Nvidia fell about 2.5%, AMD lost 6%, and Micron sank about 3.5%. A trillion dollars is the sort of sum that usually requires a war or a decade, and the market managed it between Monday and Thursday.

The sell-off spread well beyond Wall Street. SK Hynix dropped more than 10% in Seoul, Samsung Electronics fell 8.73%, and in Tokyo Advantest plunged almost 14%. In Europe, ASML was down 5.2% and ASM International 8.6%. Taiwan's TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, fell a comparatively polite 1.81%.

The first culprit is the cost of money. Wednesday's U.S. inflation data came in hotter than expected, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to 26,692.87 while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to 7,718.94. Official data show the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.21% and inflation at 3.74% a year. Translation: the government now pays investors a solid 5% to lend it money, which makes a risky bet on data centers have to try harder.

That matters because, as CNBC reported, the chief executives of Broadcom and Intel warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind for AI. Broadcom's Hock Tan said it could be a bigger challenge than shortages of chips or electricity. Building AI infrastructure is expensive, and expensive things get more so when borrowed at higher rates. MarketWatch added that reported details about Anthropic's financial progress are feeding worries about the health of the AI ecosystem, though its excerpt gave no specifics.

Memory chips took the worst of it. Over five days, SK Hynix plunged 26%, Samsung tanked 22% and Micron dropped around 11%. The trigger was ChangXin Memory Technologies, a Chinese chipmaker, announcing a server memory product on a new architecture that could pack in more data. Investors concluded that Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron might lose market share, which is a lot to conclude from an announcement.

Analysts were less alarmed. Ben Barringer of Quilter Cheviot noted that if yields are only 50%, you are literally putting half the chips in the bin. Translation: making a chip once is not the same as making millions profitably. Kevin Cassidy of Rosenblatt said of CXMT's progress: "We don't think this is going to swing the supply-demand equation at all."

Then came 2029. A South Korean newspaper column cited two experts expecting a "flood of new supply" that would turn the memory market into a red ocean that year, and Elon Musk replied on X that China would be making "a LOT of RAM in 2028." CNBC noted that no other analysts have echoed a forecast that far out. The market responded to a prediction about 2029 by selling in 2026, which is either foresight or enthusiasm for round numbers.

There is a more sober case. Memory has historically boomed when demand outran supply and busted when factories caught up, and factories take three to five years to build. Counterpoint Research sees DRAM prices falling about 23% in 2028 from 2027, yet still roughly 230% above 2025. It also points to three- to five-year long-term agreements with upfront payments and price floors and ceilings, which should soften any downturn. A bust where prices are still more than three times higher is a bust few industries would complain about.

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives called the pullback a buying opportunity, saying "rates are a financing question, not a demand question." He said he would worry about cuts to hyperscaler spending, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices. None of those has been reported yet. For now the market is panicking about the price of the loan rather than the thing it buys, which is at least a specific kind of panic.
articles.wire_headline: Nvidia, AMD, Micron fall as AI stock sell-off deepens

articles.headline: U.S. Deficit Hits $2 Trillion as Treasury Tells IMF to Check Its Own Homework
articles.dek: With 10-year yields above 5% and debt past $40 trillion, the Treasury's answer to a warning about growth is a list of the IMF's old forecasting errors.
articles.catch_up: U.S. government debt has passed $40 trillion, the deficit is running near $2 trillion, and long-term Treasury yields have climbed above 5% since the war with Iran began on Feb. 28. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the U.S. can grow its way out, and the IMF says it cannot.
articles.why_it_matters: The 10-year Treasury yield sets the tone for mortgage rates, which are around 7.5%, and for what the government pays to borrow. Higher rates make the deficit harder to shrink, and the politics for fixing it look stuck for at least two years.
body: The U.S. federal deficit for fiscal 2026 will come in near $2 trillion, CNBC reported, and the Treasury is due to publish the official figure in the next few days. The Congressional Budget Office estimated $1.993 trillion, which works out to roughly 6.0% to 6.2% of GDP. Bessent has said the target should be below 4% by the end of President Trump's term, which CNBC describes as something the country has almost no chance of hitting.

The bond market has noticed. The 10-year Treasury yield closed Wednesday at 5.19%, up 123 basis points since the end of February. Translation: a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so lenders now demand about 1.2 percentage points more than they did before the war. Official data put it at 5.21% on Oct. 13, against a Fed funds rate of 3.88%.

CNBC lists several causes. The Iran war pushed up oil and diesel prices, which makes bond traders worry that the Federal Reserve will raise rates. The government keeps issuing debt, and companies are issuing hundreds of billions more to build artificial intelligence infrastructure. Translation: the Treasury is no longer the only borrower asking for money, and investors can pick among borrowers.

Ordinary people feel this through mortgages. The average 30-year fixed rate is hovering around 7.5%, and Redfin said pending home sales fell 4% in September, the biggest monthly drop in three years. Mortgage rates follow the 10-year yield, so the Treasury's borrowing problem becomes a household's down-payment problem.

The debt arithmetic gets worse as rates rise. The CBO estimates that rates a half-point above its forecast would add $1.9 trillion to deficits over 10 years, and 1.5 points above would add $6 trillion. The agency expects the 10-year to average 4.3%, against 5.3% today, so the good scenario requires yields to fall by a full point.

Bessent's answer is growth. 'We have to grow our way out of it,' he said in Dallas last month, and he and others point to AI as the engine. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget calculates that growth alone would need a decade of 7.2% annual expansion to balance the budget. Second-quarter GDP was just revised up to 2.2% annualized, so the plan requires more than tripling it and keeping it there.

The IMF's Kristalina Georgieva said in Bangkok that strong U.S. growth would not be enough to put debt on a sustainable path. David Zervos, the newly appointed counselor to the Treasury Secretary, replied by email that readers should remember 'how messy their forecasts have been.' He cited 2008, Southeast Asia in 1997, Russia in 2022 and Argentina. Translation: the Treasury is not arguing with the arithmetic, only with the person who did it.

Politics offers little help. Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House in the Nov. 3 midterms, and Trump has pledged $5,000 checks to every adult citizen if they sweep. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next House speaker, wants to reverse $1 trillion in healthcare cuts. CNBC notes that divided government sometimes produces compromises, but the two sides start far apart.

Across the Atlantic, France offers a preview of how this goes. Its parliament begins debating the 2027 budget Tuesday, its borrowing costs are the highest in nearly 25 years, and student protests are making consolidation unpopular. INSEAD's Antonio Fatas says the ECB 'will not save a country that cannot save itself.' CNBC stresses that high borrowing costs are not yet a crisis, since higher yields also attract buyers to Treasuries.

Markets, for now, are calm: the S&P 500 stood at 7,718.94 on Oct. 14 and the VIX at 16.87. The kicker is that investors are relaxed about a problem that, by CNBC's account, only politics can fix, and politics is the one asset nobody is currently issuing.
articles.wire_headline: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge

articles.headline: IMF Raises Growth Forecast, Credits AI Boom, Warns Everything Else Is Held Together With Tape
articles.dek: The fund now sees 3.1% global growth in 2026, but says the buffers that absorbed the Hormuz shock are running out and AI enthusiasm is doing a lot of the lifting.
articles.catch_up: The IMF released its latest World Economic Outlook at its annual meetings in Bangkok, amid a Middle East war that has disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and pushed up energy costs. The fund nudged global growth up from July's forecast, mostly because of AI investment.
articles.why_it_matters: The cushion keeping energy prices and markets calm is thinning, while borrowing costs sit at multidecade highs. If AI spending disappoints, the IMF says U.S. stocks could fall 20%, which would reach well beyond people who own AI shares.
body: The International Monetary Fund raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% from 3% in July, according to CNBC, which is still below last year's 3.5%. The fund kept its 2027 forecast at 3.4%. It credited the improvement to AI-related investment, and then spent the remaining pages explaining why that is not entirely reassuring.

The headline message from Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF's economic counsellor, was that the global economy has been resilient but that resilience is "reaching its limits." Translation: the world has been paying for this war with savings, and the account balance is visible from here.

The savings in question are buffers. Governments diversified fuel sources and tapped strategic reserves, which the IMF says contained the turmoil from the war. But global oil reserves are being drawn down by about 2.7 million barrels a day, close to levels that could trigger sharp price moves. The latest data show Brent crude at $125.44, which suggests the buffer is working in the sense that it could be worse.

The fund now expects the Strait of Hormuz to reopen in March next year and return to its pre-war state by October. In July it had assumed a reopening by mid-July. Gulf crude exports averaged 88% of pre-conflict levels in September. Inflation is forecast at 4.7% this year and 4.1% in 2027, up from 3.9% previously. The fund also puts the odds of global inflation topping 5% in 2027 at about 35%, up from 30% in April.

Growth is also lopsided. Thirty-two economies now account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April. Taiwan is forecast to grow 10.7% and South Korea 3.3%, both on chip demand. India leads the major economies at 7.0%, and the U.S. is at 2.3%. The euro zone is expected to manage 1.1%, and the Middle East and Central Asia region is projected to contract 0.3%, with Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit declines before double-digit rebounds in 2027. China is forecast at 4.5%. In the IMF's words, growth is being "reallocated" according to exposure to the war and to AI demand. Translation: your forecast depends on whether you sell energy-hungry things or buy them.

The AI boom, meanwhile, is both the rescue and the risk. The IMF called it a "large, front-loaded demand shock": money pouring into chips, data centers and power generation before productivity gains have shown up. It also said calm financial markets may partly reflect "AI-related exuberance." If profit and productivity hopes are reassessed and the gains fail to appear, the fund's scenario has U.S. equities down 20% and global growth 1.1% below baseline by 2028. The S&P 500 stood at 7718.94 on Oct. 14, so there is a considerable distance to fall.

Then there is the bill. Advanced-economy benchmark yields are at multidecade highs, and tech companies borrowing to fund AI are adding to the pressure. The 10-year Treasury yield was 5.21% on Oct. 13. Translation: governments and companies are competing for the same borrowed money, and lenders have noticed. The IMF projects advanced-economy public debt reaching 115% of GDP by 2031, up from 108% in 2025.

Its prescription is predictable and not cheap. Governments should rebuild fiscal space, keep household energy support "temporary, targeted, and nondistortionary," and keep monetary policy "sufficiently restrictive." Central bank independence is critical, Tenreyro said, as governments face financing pressure. Asking governments to spend less during a war, an energy shock and a defense buildup is the sort of advice that is easy to endorse and hard to attend.
What to watch: the oil drawdown, the reopening date for Hormuz, and whether anyone in the AI supply chain begins to mention profits.
articles.wire_headline: IMF sees milder global slowdown as AI boom offsets war hit — warns resilience is nearing limits
